lecture_subjects: Time as root cause of failure
Trial and error in early-stage building
english_transcription:
Time and Money

SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 14

Given February 2nd, 2025, by Yonatan Stern


The VCs themselves say that 1 out of 10 succeeds. And if 1 out of 10 succeeds, they do so well that they cover the expense of all the other nine that failed and even make more money. So from the VC perspective, they are a great success. The question is, what about the founders, what about the companies? If you look at the same sentence spelled slightly differently — not one out of ten succeeds, but nine out of ten fail — that starts to be much more interesting. Nine out of ten companies fail. The question of course is, why do they fail?

CB Insights did a survey of 101 companies and got these answers. Don't worry about reading them, but if you add up all the percentages you will realize that we get to about 300%. If you get to about 300%, I would assume that many people filled in at least three answers or something like that. There are many reasons. And when there are many reasons and people give you a lot of answers, basically they don't have the real answer. They blame this and they blame that — the market wasn't ready, the market was full, and all of that. So many answers means there is no single answer for why they fail.

Let's look at it from the VC firms' perspective. They see hundreds of companies every year. When we talk to them, it's anywhere between 200 to 300 to 1,000 companies that they talk to or see every year. At the end, they invest in somewhere between two to four companies every year. So they do due diligence, they interview, they check, and in the end they choose two to three out of a few hundred — just to make sure they invest in the top companies. However they do the selection and the screening, they clearly look for superb teams with extraordinary talent. They interview them, they do due diligence, and look for a huge potential market and a disruptive solution for a big problem. These are their criteria, and they put the team as number one. So they choose the best of the best — and yet 9 out of 10 fail. 9 out of 10 fail. So if 90% of well-funded, talented teams fail, there must be a root cause. You can't really blame everybody as an idiot. Let's just be realistic.

They chose the best people possible, they poured tons of money into them, they believed this was a huge problem, they believed there was a market, that they had a great solution — and 9 out of 10 fail. There must be something far more fundamental that caused all of these companies to fail. So the root cause, in my mind, can be summed up in one word: time. They basically don't have enough time to succeed. Really, if you look at it — if you look at all the answers that people gave — at the end of the day, they just didn't have enough time to succeed. Because building a new company from scratch is a very long process. Many of you here have done it already and you know how much effort goes into it. And a lot of it is trial and error.

Because you're doing something new, it's a new team. You hire people — people are difficult. You talk to potential customers, they don't know what you're talking about. You don't understand how to sell, how to package what the product does. A gazillion things that are trial and error. And when you do so many trials and errors every day, it takes time, because the error takes time. What you see here is that the whole process of building a startup takes a lot of time — but they don't have the time. Why? Because the VC investors don't have the time their model talks about. They need to return the money to their investors. What we call a VC firm is just a management company — the money is not their money. They take money from insurance companies and things like that.

So in their charter, they need to return the money with all the profits — the great profits — within seven to ten years. That's the money they have. Now, how do you return money? You got money, you need to return money. To return money, you need to take the company you invested in and convert it back to money. So you get money, put it in the company, get shares — now you need to get those shares back to money. That's how it works. So there are only two ways of taking money out of the company in a big way. One is being acquired — somebody buys the entire company and pays you money. Or you go and do an IPO, an initial public offering, preferably on the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq — and then you liquidate the shares. Essentially, people can take every share and sell it and convert it to money on an instantaneous basis. That's an exit.

So VCs need you to move from an idea and two founders to being acquired or doing an IPO within seven to ten years. That's the time allotted to you. So let's think about going public. To go public on the US stock exchange — there are only about six or seven thousand companies on the exchange, that's it. They typically require that you have about $100 million in revenues, growing by about 20% year over year. And profitability — it used to be that in 2020-21, they didn't need you to be profitable. Now everybody says you have to be profitable, so they went back to: yes, profitability is good. So that's what you need to do.

Very big exits usually happen when companies go public in the USA. So let's do a reality check on Israeli companies — venture-backed Israeli companies. Since the year 2000 — and I'm sorry, there are so many zeros in here, one of them is a date, the year 2000 — about 1,000 companies were founded every year. That's kind of the number we hear from IVC. That gives you, over the 24 years from 2000 to 2024, about 20,000 companies. I put it down a little bit. In that period, fewer than 100 companies went public in the US, and of them, only about 38 companies had a value on the day of the IPO of more than $100 million. That's all. And if you look even deeper — 24 of those 38, so two-thirds of those 38 companies, did it during the heyday years of 2020 to 2022. That's it. So in the 20 years before that, only 12 to 14 companies went public. It's that hard. It's not 1 in 10, it's 1 in 500. And these numbers are public so we can verify them. 1 in 500 — 499 didn't go public.

What about M&A? Companies get acquired for many reasons. Number one is they are bought for their business success. So if a company is profitable, is growing, is generating cash — it's a good asset you can sell. So companies are acquired for being a good business, and that's the easiest reason to sell a company. Or they have a unique technology or product that the buyers need. For example, it happened a lot in cybersecurity — the big players like Check Point and Palo Alto; a new company builds a product, there's a new wave of something, and they basically just buy the technology or the company. But that is much more limited, because when you develop such a technology or product, you have a handful of buyers — that's it. So they either buy you or they don't. Your selection is very minimal — there are maybe five to ten companies that might be acquirers, or the company is in trouble and sells for almost nothing.

So a lot of those companies spend $10-15 million developing a product, run out of money, are about to close, and somebody comes in and scoops them up. And at the top end, there are buyers who actually buy the company just for the team. That's it — instead of going and hiring a team, they buy the company for a few million dollars and take the whole team. And there are many other reasons. Most acquisitions are done without disclosing the deal value or the structure. So there's a press release talking very nicely about the strategic fit of the acquisition — yeah, don't laugh — but never mentioning any money involved. That probably means it's not a billion dollars, because when things are that big, you hear about it. So most of those are under the radar. And we are now doing research with IVC — IVC is the Israeli Venture Capital research firm that tracks all venture capital investments. We hope to get their data and see what really happened with all the M&As.

Okay, so why do companies fail? Basically, because they run out of money. To achieve a meaningful exit in such a short time, VC firms encourage companies to grow as fast as possible. They only have seven to ten years, starting with two people. The two of you start a company, you get some money, and they tell you: we need to get an exit, so start working. And to support that growth, the VCs invest large amounts of money — really crazy amounts of money. And I use the word "encourage," which is polite, but it's usually less polite. They tell people: go hire a team, start building, and move, move, move. And another person is starting to laugh over there — everyone who's been in that situation knows the process.

So what they want you to do is, first of all, hire an engineering team to develop the product. They want a full organization that can support growth and scale up. So they want a CFO, a VP of Marketing, a CMO, a CPO, whatever — all the C-suite roles in the world. CxO — you can put anything from A to Z: product management, marketing. You basically build it all. But why do they run out of money? You can either raise money all the time or you can start selling and making money. But the problem is that the time is too short, so they usually don't scale up sales fast enough.

So what happens is — let's say they did everything right and they're selling, say, three to four million dollars a year, but their expenses are $10 million a year. They run out of money. So they're on the path to success and they run out of money. I asked some people, "Why do companies fail?" And they said, "There's only one answer — they run out of money." I said, "But why do they run out of money?" So that's what I explained.

I want all of you to understand one thing here. And you said it. Companies move along two parallel, interdependent dimensions: time and money. These are not separate axes — they are parallel. Time and money are interchangeable all the time. Money can buy you time — not when you are old, that doesn't work — but if you are a company, money can buy you time, and definitely the other way around as well. So they need time to develop the product, to figure out marketing and sales, and to grow revenues until it covers the costs. And they need money to pay for all of that. So they hire the team, they need money to pay for all of this — and what do they do? They raise another round of financing. That's why you see companies go: pre-seed, then seed, then Round A, then Round B, then Round C. Why do they need so many rounds? Because they ran out of money — or they ran out of money and shut down, or they get acquired. A lot of these things happen because they have no choice. Not because they want to — they just have no choice. They are spending money, they need to get money, or else they shut down.

So let's see where the money goes. I like to do some spreadsheets just to show you how quickly things add up. Assume that the company raised $5 million. My question is: how long will it live? Assume each employee earns 30,000 shekels per month — just an average. Then we need to add the employer costs, so you add all the benefits — another 30% on top of it — and you're now at 39,000 shekels. Salaries are about 75% of the expenses, because you also need an office, tea, and all kinds of things. So it comes to 50,000 shekels per employee per month.
The question is, how long will it live? So assume each employee earns 30,000 shekels per month — just an average. And then we need to add the employer overhead costs, so you add all the benefits — another 30% on top of it. You are now at 39,000 shekels. Salaries are about 75% of the expenses, because you need an office, you need tea, you need all kinds of things. So it's 50,000 shekels.

And converting to dollars, the annual cost per employee is about $175,000 a year. We all know it's around less than $200,000 a year. So that's about it. Money is time, time is money. Here you can see it. If you have 30 people, that's all — you have one year to live. That's it. One year to live. Money runs really fast with people. If you only have five people, you can live for six years. If you have 50 people, you just live seven months. I put the colors in. So if you are in the green, that's okay. If you are below that, I didn't put red because it was just too alarming. But yeah, time is money and it runs really fast.

So the question is, why not raise a lot of money but spend just a trickle? That's what I would do, right? I would raise $10 million and then spend $5 a day. Don't even eat. But why don't people do it? And the answer is interesting. The more money a company raises, the higher the investor pressure to invest it faster. Why? Because they need an ROI, and they need an ROI on a bigger amount. So if an investor puts in $20 million, they now need to return 50 or 60. So the pressure to move fast is even higher. The more money they raise, the higher the pressure — not the other way around. So it doesn't help to raise a lot of money in this case. And raising initial rounds depends on three factors.

Number one: when you go to raise a Round B, let's say, the new investors don't have any existing investment in this, so they are free to make a decision. They ask: why should we invest? What have you done with the previous money? What milestones have you achieved? Do you already have customers? Do you already have revenues? Do you already have a working product? So you can raise money only at very specific points during the life of a company. And if you run out of money between those two points, you're in bad shape. It depends on market conditions — in 2008, you couldn't raise anything. 2020 was difficult. In one of the presentations I showed you the good years and the bad years. But there are years when people just don't invest.

The market is crazy. And another thing is that the market moves from one fad to the next every three or four years. Today they invest in cryptocurrency, tomorrow in cyber, and the day after in AI. The fad of the day, the week, the year. So if you happen to be from five years ago, you're not interesting to anybody anymore. That's it. Your time is done, the door is closed on that. So in most cases, additional rounds become harder and harder. Every time you raise money, there is more money on the table and you need to prove what you've done with it. The risks grow higher and they heavily dilute the founders.

So if you are the founder, even if the company ultimately succeeds, your share of the company might go down to 2%, 5%, something like that. So why fail if you can succeed? Now that I've shown you why 9 out of 10 fail, the question is: what do we do? How can we change this?

So the first thing is to change the goal of the company from an exit — a finite game — to an infinite game. What is a finite game? A finite game is a game with clear rules, a beginning and an end, winners and losers. Soccer, basketball, hockey — they start, they end. Winners, losers, two groups, clear rules. That's a finite game. This is playing a finite game: I put money in you today, and in seven to ten years you have an exit. We take the company, we sell it, we fire you, and we take the money back. Those are the rules of the game.

What is an infinite game? An infinite game is life. Why does nobody want to see the end? It's very simple. We all strongly believe — each and every one of you — that we will live forever. We live our lives with that feeling. So when I build a company, my plan is that the company will live forever, will live after me — SmartUp will live after me. That's the whole idea. So I think long term. I think about what are the most important things I want to accomplish, or that the company should accomplish. That's an infinite game.

You need to change the goal of the company from an exit to being profitable as early as possible. So instead of thinking, "I have to have an exit in seven years," you ask: how do I become profitable? Because when I become profitable, I don't need to raise more money. I'm independent, I'm a grown-up, I can buy my lunch. I don't need anybody to help me. Profitability means that every month your sales generate more money than your expenses. It's really simple. What you really want is at the end of the month, you sold $250,000, it came into the bank, and you spent $150,000 on salaries and rent and everything. That's what we mean by profitability — cash flow positive, month after month.

Profitability guarantees that your company can survive because you don't depend on any outside investor. You depend on your customers, obviously, so don't mess that up. But you are independent. The interesting thing is — and I can talk about this from experience — that when your company is growing and is profitable, it has a much more lucrative exit. And why is that? Two reasons. Three reasons. Number one, you can have the exit whenever you want because you're not dependent on anybody. You'll naturally choose a good time to do it, and you have much more room to figure out who you want to sell the company to. Second, the company has two different value components. Number one is the cash it generates. If the company generates a million dollars a month, $12 million a year, it's worth at least 20 times net. So it's $250 million before you even do anything. That's the price. You don't need to think about it. Second, there is the value of the technology or the product to the buyer, which is usually bigger than the cash, because you complement something and they can justify buying you.

I'll give you an example I saw with my own eyes. Let's say the people who buy you are a public company and they get 50 times the profit. So that means every dollar of profit they acquire from you is worth $50 to them. So clearly they'll be happy to pay you $30 on every dollar of profit, because then they make another 20 — day one. So you will see that having a profitable company is tremendously valuable.

Changing your goal will greatly increase your chance of success. The question is, what is a successful company? We at SmartUp define success as three things: it's profitable, it's fast growing, and built with a modest investment. I specifically didn't put a number — what is modest? It depends. But it's in the low millions of dollars. A million, half a million, maybe 3 million, maybe 5 million. But definitely not 20 or 30 or 50 million. And you need to be profitable and fast growing.

How do you get there? If you decide to change your company's objective from an exit to profitability, it will have an impact on everything the company does. Because just saying "change the objective" means nothing. The question is, how do I get to profitability? And that will have a dramatic, deep impact on everything you're going to do. I'm going to give you a list.

First of all, focus on sales. Day one, keep expenses to the absolute minimum. As I wrote before, the equation is: sales minus expenses equals profit. Make the expenses small, the sales high, and you're profitable. Second-grade math. Keep expenses low and focus on sales. From day one, start thinking: how can I generate income?

The sequence of activities will change. At the end of the day, we have to decide what we do and when. It changes completely — where your focus is at the beginning. Instead of building the product, you want to do branding. And I'll explain what that means. Product development will come next. The markets you want to go after — everyone in VC says, "Oh, we need a big market." We'll talk about that. No — take a beachhead. A beachhead means a small market you can penetrate easily. Jobs to be done — that's what you sell. You sell a solution. You sell a product, but not really — you sell a solution. That's the job to be done. And I'll give more information later. Contrary to what you hear, it's better not to be first. The products you develop — do you want to be disruptive or incremental? I'm giving you a list and I'll go through each one later. The team you build, who and when do you hire, the business model, pricing, packaging, the complete product, the pace your company grows. Growth engines — I'll explain the concept of a growth engine. Low-cost CAC — CAC means customer acquisition cost.

So as you can see, there is a long list of things that every company has to think about and discuss that are going to be impacted by the decision to become profitable.

So where can you learn all of that? That's where SmartUp Academy comes in. This is a program to teach the profession of building successful companies. It's a profession — you can learn it, you can understand it. The same way I described why companies fail, I can explain what you need to do to be successful. And the three pillars, as I said, are: profitable, fast growing, and with a modest investment. How do you build a fast-growing company with a modest investment? There's a course — we call it the Foundation Course. It's a 14-week intensive course. You can see all the materials on our website, and there is a registration form. All of you are encouraged to fill it out and we will get back to you.

Let's look a little bit deeper into what I said before. Each one of those topics is usually a lecture or two in the course.

Branding first. What do companies do today? Virtually all companies start by building their product. First thing they do is raise money and start building the product, assuming they have nothing to sell before they have at least a prototype. When I go to talk to someone, I have to have something in my hand to show them. You hire a team — what else can you do? A team of engineers, programmers, whatever it is.

The problem with hiring is that you create a fixed and growing expense. Each employee wants a salary, and they want it on the first of the month, for whatever reason. And you can't tell them, "We ran out of money this month, let's forget it, we'll talk next week." It doesn't work that way. You can't hire and fire and hire and fire the same person. It is the most fixed expense you will ever have. But that's what companies do. They hire a development team, which is usually a very expensive team, and they live in this belief. Those of you who saw the movie Field of Dreams know the main idea: if you build it, they will come — somehow, miraculously.
About next week. It doesn't work this way. You can't hire and fire and hire and fire the same person. It is the most fixed expense you will ever have. But that's what companies do. They hire a development team, which is usually a very expensive team, and they live in this. Those of you who saw the movie Field of Dreams — the main thing is: if you build it, they will come. Somehow, miraculously.

If you build this baseball field, all the great heroes of the past will come out of their grave and play on your baseball team. So in reality — it's not an American movie — they don't come. And you can't sell if nobody ever heard about you. That's the reality. You develop the product, it's phenomenal. You can demo it to yourself and your friends, but if nobody else ever saw it, nobody is going to buy it. Developing a product is much easier than selling it. I know it rubs engineers the wrong way, but it's much easier to develop a product than to sell it. Why? Because developing a product, everything is under your control. You sit in front of the computer and you decide what you do, and that's about it.

When you try to sell, you sit in front of the customer and you tell them what they need to do, and they just don't do it. They just don't do it. They tell you, "Oh, it was great meeting you. Thank you so much. Don't call us, we'll call you." And you can't debug them. And it takes time to educate the market, regardless of how much you try to teach. Remember, we're now talking about markets. We're not talking about a single buyer. So it takes a long time to reach your potential customers and educate them. And the only way to do it so that they are ready by the time you have the product is if you start early. It's just a matter of time. It's really that simple.

If you start talking to people about what you do today, two years from now or three years from now, when you have a product to sell, hopefully they already start thinking about you. It takes a long time. So this is a very classical marketing funnel, or sales funnel. And the first stage here is awareness. Awareness is branding. That's what awareness is. I know about you — and usually how I explain to people the difference between branding and marketing is the following. Who knows about the Kardashians? I see that all of you know about them, right? What do you know about them? But you know, right? They exist. Now I'll ask you: who is the CEO of Ford Motors? Who is the CEO of Mercedes-Benz? Who is the CEO of Tesla? Right. Why do you know the Tesla CEO? Because he's a genius at branding. That's all.

He's the brand. Okay, but you see the difference. Same type of people, but some of them were able to penetrate our cluttered heads. We know them, we heard about them, and others we don't. And their success rates reflect that. That's the point I'm trying to make. Their success rate at penetrating our brain, our mind, reflects their business success. So if you run a company, start thinking about that all the time. How do I get to the point where my potential customers know about me? They don't need to know a lot. They just don't. So instead of building the product — remember, we're in the early days. You got $200,000 from an angel investor. What are you going to do with the $200,000?

Instead of hiring somebody to build a mockup or whatever, my suggestion is: start thinking about branding activities. Start thinking about a branding growth engine. The biggest innovation you're going to make in your life is how to become a Kardashian. And many of you are missing some parts of that. But that's the biggest innovation you can think of, because that will make you successful. I don't say it's easy, but I say it's really important. And most companies don't even think about it. Strong branding will create tangible value in various ways. A much larger top of the funnel — the more people know about you, the easier it is to bring them in. It reduces the cost of sales, because once people know about you, they will respond to you.

You don't need to spend a lot of time getting them to pick up the phone, read your email, or fill out a form. You gain a deeper understanding of the market because you start talking to these people way before you build your product. And if there's a word I hate in companies, it's the word "pivot." Companies spend millions of dollars, develop a product, come to the market, and nobody wants it. Now you figure out nobody wants it? Why didn't you try to sell the product before that? It doesn't have to work. But if everybody says "oh yeah, interesting" and walks away, then you know you don't have a market. And you identify potential market beachheads.

Many times when you start doing branding, you realize there is something else that these prospects or customers want that you might be able to deliver — just because you talked to the market and people told you what they need. And obviously if you raise more money, it will make it easier. It's much easier to come in with a brand people recognize. That's why, for example, Venrock invested in ZoomInfo many years ago — mainly because the investor said, "If I hear about a company three times, I have to invest in it. And I heard about you three times."

The markets you target — VCs always tell you, you need a huge market, a very big market. Well, there isn't a big market. Never. There are a lot of little islands that together represent the big market. The example I like to give is: I have a great idea how to become rich. I know that the Chinese like rice. So all I need to do is sell one kilo of rice to every Chinese person once a year. That's all. It's really simple. And usually people start laughing. Why? Because they immediately realize the problem is not the rice. How are you going to get to a billion Chinese people and sell them rice? That's the problem. So a big market is a big problem. It's not a good thing, it's a bad thing, because it's very difficult to go after a big market. It's much easier to go after a small, well-defined market.

When the Allies wanted to conquer Europe back from the Germans, they didn't spread across 2,000 miles of Atlantic coastline. They went to one place — D-Day. That's it. 20 kilometers. That's all they wanted to conquer. 20 kilometers. That's a beachhead. You want to find the easiest point to penetrate the market and start from there. So selling to a small market segment is enough to make your company profitable. Remember what we're talking about — you want to be profitable, you're in the early stages of your company. Let's say your expenses are $300,000 a month, $4 million a year. You don't need a huge market to generate $5 million in sales. You don't. It's a small market. You pick a beachhead, you penetrate it, and you at least bring your company to profitability.

That's what you need to do at the beginning. And then it's much easier — as the Allies proved in World War II — to move from town to town, from city to city, from segment to segment. And by the way, how you segment the market can vary in many different ways. When I say segment the market, you decide how you do it. Because when you're doing the branding, you see who is responding to you, and you don't need to think about how to address a huge market. As I said, you can start small and become profitable. Better not to be first — again, everybody says you have to be first to conquer the market. Two mistakes: you don't need to conquer the market, and you don't need to be first. So being first is overrated.

I just read a book about innovation, and every other page it says innovation is incremental and evolves over time. I can bring you examples from here to wazoo — virtually all of the innovations we see today took anywhere from 10 to 100 years to evolve, and many people were involved. Let other companies educate the market. It's very expensive to educate the market. CRM — I started my business life in 1983 or so, and there was already a CRM. It was called ACT! with an exclamation mark. I think it's still alive. Nobody knew about it. Salesforce came many years later. Only today is it kind of obvious: to start a company, you need a CRM. But it took 50 years. That's what it took. Google, Facebook, WhatsApp, Amazon, Intel — you name them. They were never the first.

In the course that we give, I show you many examples of how many companies existed before each one of these giants. They learned from what other people did — what was right, what was wrong — and then they succeeded. So you don't need to be first, but you should strive to be the best. That's the point. Let other people open the market for you. Let them spend a lot of money educating the market, pour money into things, and then see how you can do it better than them. And what is the full product? The devil is always in the details. If you think about successful companies, you see they are always very focused on the details. Take Amazon, for example.

You want to return something, you just return it — no questions asked — and they refund you right away. Why? Because if they have to track the return, figure out whether you really returned it, verify that it's actually the product you bought — they spend so much money on it. It's much easier to just say, "Tell me you returned it, and I'll give you the money." And everybody's excited about it. But they're smart. So the devil is always in the details. Companies succeed or fail on the details.

Jobs to be done. My favorite writer, Clayton Christensen — he passed away from cancer about five years ago. He wrote The Innovator's Dilemma, and then the second book, The Innovator's Solution. And in that book he talks about jobs to be done. There's also another book called Competing Against Luck. The idea is: understanding customers does not drive innovation success. Understanding customer jobs does — and that's the jobs-to-be-done approach. I'll explain in a moment what it is.

So what is the jobs-to-be-done methodology? It's based on the idea that people and companies buy products and services to accomplish specific jobs in their lives or business. That means they don't really want the product — they want the end result of the product. I don't need shoe polish. I need my shoes polished. That's what I need. I can buy shoe polish, I can go to a shoemaker, or I can buy new shoes — but I don't need shoe polish. I need my shoes polished. Sounds trivial, but it's not. Because once you define it this way, the product becomes less relevant than fulfilling the customer's need. And that's critical.

Why is that so critical? Because developing a product that is good enough that when customers use it they get what they want — that's not easy. However, giving them what they want, many times, is much easier. Why? Because you can insert yourself into the equation and make sure they get what they want — with the product or without the product, it doesn't matter. So understanding what they want to accomplish is really critical.

After he published his article, people repeated similar experiments in companies and saw that it works like magic. It's very much like the famous 80/20 rule.

Venture capital firms openly acknowledge that nine out of ten of their portfolio companies fail — yet these are not random bets. VCs screen hundreds of companies annually, selecting only two to four, prioritising exceptional teams, massive market potential, and disruptive solutions. Despite this rigorous filtering, the failure rate remains staggering. The lecture argues that the root cause is not poor talent or bad ideas, but a single, underappreciated constraint: time.

The VC fund model creates a structural time pressure that most founders overlook. Because VCs manage money on behalf of institutional investors, they are contractually obligated to return capital — with substantial profit — within seven to ten years. This forces portfolio companies to reach an exit, either through acquisition or IPO, within that window. Going public on a major US exchange typically requires around $100 million in revenue, consistent 20% year-over-year growth, and profitability. The data on Israeli venture-backed companies illustrates how rare this outcome is: of roughly 20,000 companies founded since 2000, fewer than 38 achieved a meaningful US IPO — and two-thirds of those occurred during the exceptional market conditions of 2020 to 2022.

A central misstep that compounds the time problem is how founders allocate early capital. Many immediately hire expensive development teams, believing that building a great product will naturally attract customers — the "Field of Dreams" fallacy. In practice, developing a product is far easier than selling it, because sales involves educating an entire market of people who have never heard of you. By the time the product is ready, there is no audience primed to receive it.

The lecture makes a compelling case for investing in branding before — or alongside — product development. Awareness is the top of the sales funnel, and building it takes years. Companies that begin communicating their vision early create a pipeline of informed prospects, reduce customer acquisition costs, and gain market intelligence that can prevent costly pivots. The Kardashian analogy is deliberately provocative: penetrating the mental landscape of potential customers is the most important innovation a founder can achieve.

On pricing, the lecture challenges the assumption that customers are price-sensitive. For unfamiliar products in new categories, buyers have no reference point, giving founders significant latitude to charge premium prices. Pricing should be tested iteratively, tiered through thoughtful packaging, and structured to favour annual upfront payments for cash flow reasons. Finally, strong customer retention — achieved by embedding a product into a customer's daily workflows and data history — is what drives renewals and sustains compounding growth over time.
